extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general educated public; writers and critics of literature and painting
extracted.subtask_description: Short critical guidance and aesthetic principles for judging and producing poems, ballads, and paintings, as discussed in 18th-century Spectator essays (qualities such as naturalness, finish, industry, and expressive countenance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Female virtues: domestic sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Female Virtues are of a Domestick Turn. The Family is the proper Province for Private Women to shine in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women should cultivate accomplishments proper to their sex (tender mothers, faithful wives) rather than engage in partisan public competitions; examples invoked include Greek prohibitions on women's attendance at Olympic games and Roman ladies contributing jewels in wartime. If women show public spirit, let it be against open enemies of faith/liberty/country rather than domestic rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid female partisan contention
rubrics_metrics.description: Women should not interest themselves in Competitions and Contentions or act as furious partizans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions against women embroiling themselves in the nation's unnatural divisions; recommends modesty and restraint, citing Pericles' advice: 'Aspire only to those Virtues that are peculiar to your Sex... think it your greatest Commendation not to be talked of one way or other.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and simplicity in popular ballads
rubrics_metrics.description: A plain simple Copy of Nature, destitute of the Helps and Ornaments of Art, can move readers by genuine and unaffected sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ballad 'Two Children in the Wood' is praised because incidents grow naturally from the subject and the tale's simplicity evokes pity despite poor language; authenticity of sentiment outweighs elegance of expression. Anti-pattern: ridiculing simple language even when feelings are genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents must grow out of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The incidents of a narrative should arise naturally from its subject and be 'the most proper to excite Pity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that contrive episodes without organic relation to their subject lose emotional force. Example: the ballad's moving incidents are effective because they are appropriate to the theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value genuine thought over elegant diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean language may disguise great sentiment, but genuine thought and unaffected taste of nature can still please.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and readers should not reject a work solely for poor phraseology if its sentiments are natural and moving; learned authorities (Dryden, Lord Dorset) and Molière are invoked to support admiring natural simplicity. Anti-pattern: dismissing natural works because of 'abject Phrase and Poorness of Expression.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should not be mere smirking vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity (as an artist-type) produces smirking, affected faces and glaring colours — an affected, petit-maître style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drawing all subjects with the same smirk or fashionable affectation; flashy, uniform ornamentation and 'glaring Colours' that prioritize showiness over truth are faults. Example negative archetype: VANITY's figures are Petits Maitres and Coquets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of imitation without understanding (Stupidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A laborious imitator who copies vanity becomes STUPIDITY — slavish copying of affectation is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying fashionable affectations without original understanding yields poor art; imitators of vanity merely reproduce its faults rather than achieve merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid grotesque distortion (Fantasque)
rubrics_metrics.description: FANTASQUE deals in chimeras, distortions, and grimaces; his most elaborate pieces are 'agreeable Monsters' and at best terrifying dreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive distortion and grotesque invention that do not serve a coherent expressive purpose lead to works that unsettle rather than truly please. Use of imaginative distortions should be purposeful, not merely bizarre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Haste and parsimony produce unfinished art (Avarice)
rubrics_metrics.description: AVARICE is hasty, leaves pictures unfinished; haste prevents proper mixing of colours and cleaning of pencils, causing beauty to fade faster than the sitter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rushed work sacrifices durability and the lasting beauty of a piece. Antipattern: prioritising speed and cheapness over careful execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry: meticulous, labourious workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: INDUSTRY produces wonderfully laboured works; when drawing a portrait he 'did not omit a single Hair in his Face' and attended to even ship tackle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoroughness and close attention to detail are virtues: careful execution, complete representation, and painstaking finish (including subtle night-pieces and handling of light) produce convincing, admiring works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-retouching and malicious refinement (Envy)
rubrics_metrics.description: ENVY retouches fine pieces but produces no originals, aggravating features, loading defects, and poisoning colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retouching or criticism that exaggerates faults does harm; excessive corrective intervention that accentuates flaws rather than improving should be avoided. Anti-pattern: editors or critics who 'aggravated every Feature that was before over-charged.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Time improves and mellows art
rubrics_metrics.description: TIME, by repeated, light touches, wears off disagreeable gloss, adds a beautiful Brown to the Shades, and mellowness to the Colours; he makes every Picture appear more perfect than when fresh from the Master's Pencil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patience and the passage of time can enrich and harmonize a work's tones and effects; premature judgment or display may miss the value added by maturation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy: the 'air' of the face over features
rubrics_metrics.description: We may be better known by our Looks than by our Words; 'the Air of the whole Face is much more expressive than the Lines of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging character/temper, attend to the overall countenance and expressive air rather than isolated features; the general look conveys inward disposition. Anti-pattern: over-reliance on isolated features or forced analogies (likening faces to animals) without regard for the overall expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial expression as immediate index of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Passion gives a particular Cast to the Countenance and is apt to discover itself in some Feature or other; lovers often 'complain, resent, languish, despair, and die in dumb Show.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that emotions often manifest visually and that silent, nonverbal expression can convey strong states; useful for portraitists and character-drawers to capture these airs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should be able to admire nature's simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those endowed with true greatness of soul and genius can divest themselves of ridicule and admire Nature in her Simplicity and Nakedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages critics to cultivate generosity of taste and to value natural simplicity rather than show off pedantic fault-finding; 'little conceited Wits' who only find fault miss significant beauties.
